author: Origen of Alexandria
occasion: Origen explains why he undertook to examine the doctrines of heretics and the claims of Greek philosophers about truth: as his reputation spread, both heretics and those trained in Greek learning, especially philosophy, came to him. He did this in imitation of Pantaenus, and he also mentions Heraclas, now a presbyter of Alexandria, as a related figure whom he found at the teacher of philosophical learning.
argument: Origen describes how, because of his growing reputation, heretics and people trained in Greek philosophy came to him. He therefore decided to examine both heretical doctrines and what philosophers claimed to teach about truth. He did this following the example of Pantaenus, who had helped many and had considerable preparation in these matters. He also mentions Heraclas, now a presbyter of Alexandria, whom he found at the teacher of philosophical learning, already having spent five years with him before Origen began to attend those lectures. Heraclas had exchanged common clothing for the philosopher's garb, which he still keeps, and he continues to study Greek books as much as he can.

outline.move: Origen states that because of his reputation, heretics and those trained in Greek philosophy came to him, so he decided to examine their doctrines and claims about truth.
He says he did this imitating Pantaenus, and he also mentions Heraclas, now a presbyter of Alexandria, whom he found at the teacher of philosophical learning.

He notes that Heraclas had already spent five years with that teacher before Origen began to attend those lectures, and that Heraclas had exchanged common clothing for the philosopher's garb, which he still keeps, while continuing to study Greek books.

_unresolved_facts.claim: as his reputation spread, both heretics and those trained in Greek learning, especially philosophy, came to him
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐπεὶ δὲ ἀνακειμένῳ μοι τῷ λόγῳ, τῆς φήμης διατρεχούσης περὶ τῆς ἕξεως ἡμῶν, προσῄεσαν ὁτὲ μὲν αἱρετικοί, ὁτὲ δὲ οἱ ἀπὸ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν μαθημάτων
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says 'ἀνακειμένῳ μοι τῷ λόγῳ' (while I was devoted to my study/lecture), not merely that his reputation spread. The occasion is specifically that while Origen was engaged in his own study, with his reputation circulating about his learning/condition (ἕξεως), they came to him.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He did this in imitation of Pantaenus, and he also mentions Heraclas, now a presbyter of Alexandria, as a related figure whom he found at the teacher of philosophical learning
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: μιμησάμενοί τε τὸν πρὸ ἡμῶν πολλοὺς ὠφελήσαντα Πάνταινον... καὶ τὸν νῦν ἐν τῷ πρεσβυτερίῳ καθεζόμενον Ἀλεξανδρέων Ἡρακλᾶν, ὅντινα εὗρον παρὰ τῷ διδασκάλῳ τῶν φιλοσόφων μαθημάτων
_unresolved_facts.fix: Origen imitated Pantaenus; Heraclas is not presented as someone imitated but as someone found at the teacher's school. The 'imitation' applies to Pantaenus alone, not to both figures.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He did this following the example of Pantaenus, who had helped many and had considerable preparation in these matters
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: μιμησάμενοί τε τὸν πρὸ ἡμῶν πολλοὺς ὠφελήσαντα Πάνταινον, οὐκ ὀλίγην ἐν ἐκείνοις ἐσχηκότα παρασκευήν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text says Pantaenus 'had considerable preparation in those things' (ἐν ἐκείνοις), referring to the examination of heretical doctrines and philosophical claims, not merely 'in these matters' vaguely. Also, 'πολλοὺς ὠφελήσαντα' means 'having benefited many,' not 'helped many' in a general sense but specifically having been of benefit to many people.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Heraclas had exchanged common clothing for the philosopher's garb, which he still keeps
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: δι' ὃν καὶ πρότερον κοινῇ ἐσθῆτι χρώμενος ἀποδυσάμενος καὶ φιλόσοφον ἀναλαβὼν σχῆμα μέχρι τοῦ δεῦρο τηρεῖ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The subject of ἀποδυσάμενος and ἀναλαβὼν is Heraclas, but the construction is ambiguous: 'δι' ὃν' (because of whom/which, referring to the teacher) and the participles describe Heraclas's action. However, 'κοινῇ ἐσθῆτι χρώμενος' is a concessive or temporal participle ('though/while previously using common clothing, having put it off and taken up the philosopher's garb, he keeps it to this day'). The brief's 'exchanged' is acceptable, but the causal connection 'because of whom' (the teacher) is omitted.
The form 'αὐτῷ' refers to the teacher (τῷ διδασκάλῳ), not to Heraclas. Heraclas is the one who spent five years with 'him' (the teacher). The source_forms for Heraclas should not include 'αὐτῷ'.

The sections frag-open and frag-rem-early contain identical text. The outline should recognize that frag-open contains the complete passage, while frag-rem-early, frag-rem-mid, and frag-rem-close are editorial fragments of the same text. The outline incorrectly treats frag-open and frag-rem-early as containing different content that together make a move, when they are actually duplicates/fragments of the same material.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: [section frag-rem-mid] φιλοσόφων περὶ ἀληθείας λέγειν ἐπαγγελλόμενα...
_unresolved_facts.fix: The frag-rem-mid section begins mid-sentence with 'φιλοσόφων' (genitive plural), which is the continuation of 'τῶν φιλοσόφων' from the previous clause. It does not contain a complete move but continues the sentence from frag-rem-early. The outline's division by fragments creates artificial breaks in the middle of sentences and arguments.

The frag-rem-close section begins with 'μαθημάτων' which is the continuation of 'τῶν φιλοσόφων μαθημάτων' from frag-rem-mid. This is not a separate move but the completion of the relative clause about Heraclas that began in frag-rem-mid with 'ὅντινα'.
